posts.copy:
More than 100 investors said no to Canva before one said yes.

Melanie Perkins spent about three years on that, pitching from Perth. The business did not meaningfully change between the last no and the first yes.

Two things changed.

The framing. She was asking investors to price a category that did not exist yet, so there was nothing to benchmark against. Consumer design software read as niche until the pitch stopped asking people to believe in a market and started showing them the behaviour.

And the access. The conversation that moved it happened because an investor was in Perth to kitesurf, and she got in front of him there. Not a warm intro from a fund's contact page. A room she managed to be in.

A hundred nos from the wrong list is not information about your company. It is information about your list.

That is the part of fundraising support we actually do. We cut the list, we fix who is on it, and we work the warm paths into the rooms where your story already makes sense. We do not promise the yes, because nobody honest can.

We had nothing to do with Canva. We just think it is the clearest version of this story.

If you are mid-raise: how many investors on your list have funded your category in the last 18 months?

#Fundraising #Founders #APAC #VentureStudio

posts.disclosure: We had nothing to do with Canva. We just think it is the clearest version of this story.

posts.copy:
Notion's second-biggest market outside the US was Japan before Notion had a Japanese product.

The community got there first. Japanese users ran their own meetups, built their own forums, and wrote and self-published their own books about a tool that only spoke English.

Notion localised in October 2021, after the demand already existed. In the year before that launch, daily active users in Japan grew 500%.

The unlock was sequencing, not translation.

Most Western software teams run it the other way round. Localise, then hunt for demand, then conclude the market is small when the funnel stays empty.

Notion let a market prove itself and then paid to serve it properly.

This is the part that generalises across the region. You are not entering one market, you are entering 15+ ecosystems with different rules, cultures and buyer behaviour, and only some of them are already pulling on your product. The job is working out which ones are pulling before you spend.

That is most of what our GTM advisory work actually is. Find the pull, then sequence the spend.

We have never worked with Notion. This is commentary from the outside.

Comment PULL and we will send you the three questions we use to test whether a market is pulling or you are pushing.

#GTM #APAC #MarketEntry #Japan

posts.copy:
Unitree closed its first day on the Shanghai exchange up 542%.

That is not a robotics story. It is a supply chain story wearing a robot costume.

Read from a desk in London or New York, the takeaway is either "Chinese robotics is a bubble" or "we should have bought the stock". Both miss it.

The reason a humanoid company can clear a Shanghai listing review in 73 days, and price at a 61 billion yuan valuation, is that almost everything it needs is already sitting within an hour's drive of its assembly line.

On the ground in Shenzhen this is unremarkable. Actuators on one floor. Reducers two buildings over. A machinist who will turn a revised part around before the end of the week, then argue with you about the tolerance, because they have built the same part for four other robotics firms this month.

That is the bit you cannot read in a prospectus. The company is not the moat. The one-hour radius is the moat.

We are taking a small group of operators through that radius next month.
